Slaughter of the Innocents
SLAW-ter uv the IN-oh-sents
noun phrase (Matthew 2)
The traditional name for Herod's massacre of the children of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16); “innocents” from the Latin innocentes, the guiltless little ones slain.

Biblical Definition

The slaughter of the innocents is the massacre of the male children of Bethlehem ordered by Herod the Great in his rage to destroy the newborn King. When the wise men did not return to him, Herod, exceeding wroth, sent forth and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time he had inquired of the wise men. The Lord Jesus was preserved, for the angel had warned Joseph to take the young child and His mother and flee into Egypt. Matthew sees in the weeping of Bethlehem the fulfilment of Jeremiah: “In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.” The dictionary holds the account as true history and reads it for its solemn lessons. It displays the murderous enmity of the world against Christ from His very infancy, the same enmity that pursued Him to the cross. It shows the tyrant's readiness to shed innocent blood to guard his throne, a perennial mark of ungodly power. And it sets the cost of redemption against the backdrop of grief: the King came into a world of Herods, and His coming, while it brought salvation, also provoked the rage of hell. The slaughter of the innocents stands as a witness against the shedding of innocent blood in every age, and as a reminder that the Prince of Peace was born into the world's violence, to bear it and at last to end it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Herod's massacre of the male children of Bethlehem two years old and under, in his rage to destroy the newborn King (Matthew 2:16); the world's enmity against Christ from His infancy, and the fulfilment of Rachel's weeping.

SLAUGHTER OF THE INNOCENTS, noun phrase. Herod's massacre of the children of Bethlehem to destroy the newborn Christ.

He slew all the children two years old and under in Bethlehem and its coasts (Matthew 2:16).

The Lord Jesus was preserved by the flight into Egypt (Matthew 2:13).

It fulfilled Jeremiah's “Rachel weeping for her children” (Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18).

It displays the world's murderous enmity against Christ from His infancy.

Key Scripture

Mt 2:16 — "Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men."

Mt 2:18 — "In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not."

Jer 31:15 — "Thus saith the LORD; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not."

Mt 2:13 — "And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the critical denial of its historicity and the sentimental Christmas that forgets the blood and grief into which the King was born.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the historicity of the account and the gravity of innocent blood. Some critics deny the slaughter ever happened, since no source outside Matthew records it; but the deed is wholly in character with Herod the Great, who murdered his own sons and wife to secure his throne, and the small population of Bethlehem would make the massacre a minor item in a brutal reign. The dictionary affirms the Gospel's witness: the event is true history, and the silence of pagan chroniclers proves nothing against the inspired record.

The sentimental celebration of Christmas, all light and comfort, easily forgets that the King was born into a world of violence and that His coming provoked the rage of a murderous tyrant. The slaughter of the innocents restores the shadow that lies across the manger: the enmity of the world against Christ began at His birth and pursued Him to the cross. The dictionary reads the account as a perpetual witness against the shedding of innocent blood by ungodly power, and as a reminder that the Prince of Peace entered the world's grief and bloodshed in order to bear it, to weep with the weeping, and at last to wipe away every tear.

Hebrew Roots

From “innocents” (Latin innocentes, the guiltless), the traditional name for the slain children of Bethlehem; the “coasts” (Greek horia, borders) mark the region around the town.

expand to see more

Innocentes, Latin, the guiltless, the name given the slaughtered children.

Horia, Greek, “coasts” or borders, the region of Bethlehem affected.

Herod “the Great,” the Idumean king infamous for murdering his own kin.

“Rachel weeping” (Jeremiah 31:15) is the prophetic lament Matthew sees fulfilled.

The “flight into Egypt” preserves the Christ and recalls Israel's own sojourn there.

Usage

"He defended the event as true history, noting it suited Herod's murderous reign exactly."

"She heard in Rachel's weeping a witness against the shedding of innocent blood in every age."
